DefaultTab.Hint: Which tab is active when the window opens.

Attack.Title: Attack
Attack.Subtitle: One attack roll with a weapon or an Unarmed Strike.
Attack.Summary: When you take the Attack action you make one attack roll with a weapon or an Unarmed Strike. Features such as Extra Attack let you make several attacks within the same action, and you may move between those attacks. You can also draw or stow one weapon as part of the action, before or after the attack. If you have the weapon's mastery property, you can use it with this attack.
Attack.Example: A level-5 Fighter has Extra Attack. She strikes a Goblin, moves 10 feet to the next enemy and makes her second attack there.
Attack.Notes: The Unarmed Strike offers three options: Damage, Grapple or Shove. Grapple and Shove replace the damage with an effect and are not separate actions.

Magic.Title: Magic
Magic.Subtitle: Activate a magic item or trigger an item's spell-effect that requires an action.
Magic.Summary: The Magic action covers the use of magic items whose activation requires an action — wands, scrolls, potions, and item features that explicitly call for a Magic action. It does not replace casting one of your own spells; that uses the dedicated spellcasting actions and timing rules.
Magic.Example: A Rogue draws a scroll of Identify and uses the Magic action to discharge its effect on a ring the party recovered from the vault.

Dash.Title: Dash
Dash.Subtitle: Gain extra movement equal to your current speed.
Dash.Summary: When you take the Dash action you gain extra movement for the current turn. The increase equals your Speed after applying any modifiers. If you have a special speed such as a Fly Speed or Swim Speed, you may use that instead of your normal Speed, choosing each time you take the action.
Dash.Example: A Monk with 30 feet of Speed dashes and can move up to 60 feet this turn. If his Speed were reduced to 15 feet, dashing would allow only 30 feet.

Disengage.Title: Disengage
Disengage.Subtitle: Your movement until the end of the turn does not provoke opportunity attacks.
Disengage.Summary: Disengage prevents your movement from triggering opportunity attacks until the end of your turn, in exchange for your action. Reach itself is not magically ignored — only the Opportunity Attack reaction is suppressed by this action.
Disengage.Example: A Wizard ended his last turn engaged with an Orc. Rather than risk the trip back, he Disengages and safely walks 30 ft away to cast at range.

Dodge.Title: Dodge
Dodge.Subtitle: Attacks against you have disadvantage; your Dexterity saves have advantage.
Dodge.Summary: Until the start of your next turn every attack roll against you has Disadvantage if you can see the attacker, and you make Dexterity saving throws with Advantage. You lose these benefits if you gain the Incapacitated condition or your Speed drops to 0.
Dodge.Example: A wounded Cleric facing two Goblins skips attacking and Dodges instead — both Goblins must roll their attacks against him with disadvantage this round.

Subtitle.metric: Grant an ally advantage on a roll — attack target must be within 1.5 m.
Subtitle.imperial: Grant an ally advantage on a roll — attack target must be within 5 ft.

Summary.metric: The Help action offers two options. First, you can assist an ability check: choose one of your skill or tool proficiencies and an ally you can help verbally or physically, and that ally has Advantage on their next check with it. Second, you can assist an attack roll by briefly distracting an enemy within 1.5 metres of you, giving one ally Advantage on their next attack roll against that enemy. Both benefits expire at the start of your next turn.
Summary.imperial: The Help action offers two options. First, you can assist an ability check: choose one of your skill or tool proficiencies and an ally you can help verbally or physically, and that ally has Advantage on their next check with it. Second, you can assist an attack roll by briefly distracting an enemy within 5 feet of you, giving one ally Advantage on their next attack roll against that enemy. Both benefits expire at the start of your next turn.

Example.metric: The Rogue stands adjacent to an Ogre guard. She Helps the Fighter: the Fighter's next attack against the Ogre has advantage.
Example.imperial: The Rogue stands adjacent to an Ogre guard. She Helps the Fighter: the Fighter's next attack against the Ogre has advantage.

Notes.metric: The DM decides whether your assistance is possible at all. You need the matching skill or tool proficiency to assist an ability check.
Notes.imperial: The DM decides whether your assistance is possible at all. You need the matching skill or tool proficiency to assist an ability check.

Hide.Title: Hide
Hide.Subtitle: A Dexterity (Stealth) check against DC 15.
Hide.Summary: You make a Dexterity (Stealth) check against DC 15 while you are Heavily Obscured or behind Total Cover and no enemy can see you. On a success you gain the Invisible condition. It ends as soon as you make a noise louder than a whisper, make an attack roll, cast a spell with a verbal component, or an enemy finds you.
Hide.Example: The Ranger ducks behind a wagon, rolls a 18 on Stealth, and gains the Invisible condition. The next attack from cover has advantage — but that attack also ends the hidden state.
Hide.Notes: The Invisible condition is tied to the hiding. If an enemy finds you it ends immediately, regardless of your check result.

Influence.Title: Influence
Influence.Subtitle: Get an NPC to do something via Persuasion, Deception, Intimidation, or Performance.
Influence.Summary: You describe or roleplay how you communicate with the monster, and the DM decides whether it is willing, unwilling or hesitant. A willing monster complies without a check; an unwilling one refuses without a check. Only a hesitant monster calls for a check, usually Deception, Intimidation, Performance, Persuasion or Animal Handling. The DC is 15 or the monster's Intelligence score, whichever is higher.
Influence.Example: A Bard tries to persuade a guard captain to release a prisoner. The DM rules him hesitant, so the Bard rolls Charisma (Persuasion) against DC 15.
Influence.Notes: After a failed check you must wait 24 hours before pressing the same monster in the same way again.

Ready.Title: Ready
Ready.Subtitle: Set a trigger and act later with your Reaction.
Ready.Summary: You choose a perceivable circumstance as the trigger and the action you will take in response, or movement up to your Speed. If the trigger occurs before the start of your next turn you take it with your Reaction, or you may ignore the trigger. Readying a spell means casting it immediately and spending its resources, holding its energy with Concentration until the trigger releases it.
Ready.Example: The Wizard says: when the cultist steps on the trapdoor, I cast Magic Missile. As soon as the cultist does, the Wizard spends his Reaction and the spell triggers.
Ready.Notes: A readied spell must have a casting time of one action. If your Concentration breaks first, the spell dissipates with no effect.

Search.Title: Search
Search.Subtitle: A Wisdom check to find something concealed or a hidden creature.
Search.Summary: When you take the Search action you make a Wisdom check to notice something that is not obvious. Which skill applies depends on what you are looking for: Insight for a creature's state of mind, Medicine for its ailment or cause of death, Perception for a hidden creature or object, Survival for tracks and food.
Search.Example: The Ranger investigates an abandoned watchtower, rolls 17 on Perception, and finds fresh footprints — the DM describes them as medium-size, less than an hour old.

Study.Title: Study
Study.Subtitle: An Intelligence check to recall lore or analyze a creature, object, or phenomenon.
Study.Summary: When you take the Study action you make an Intelligence check to draw on your memory, a book, a clue or another source of knowledge. Arcana covers spells, magic items and certain creatures; History covers events, civilisations and wars; Investigation covers traps, ciphers and contraptions; Nature covers terrain, flora and weather; Religion covers deities, rites and cults.
Study.Example: Facing a Gargoyle guardian, the Cleric rolls Religion via Study and recalls its weakness to bludgeoning damage — the DM grants a narrative hint.
Study.Notes: Each field of knowledge also covers certain creature types. Arcana, for instance, includes Aberrations, Constructs, Elementals, Fey and Monstrosities.

Utilize.Title: Utilize
Utilize.Subtitle: Use a nonmagical object that requires an action.
Utilize.Summary: Normally you interact with an object while doing something else, such as drawing a sword as part of the Attack action. If an object explicitly requires an action to use, you take the Utilize action. Magic items use the Magic action instead.
Utilize.Example: The Dwarf Fighter faces a rusty wall lever. He utilizes it, and the trapdoor under the troll's table swings open.

Overview.Title: Bonus Action
Overview.Subtitle: An additional, short action — only when a feature explicitly grants one.
Overview.Summary: Various class features, spells and other abilities let you take one additional action on your turn. You can take a Bonus Action only when a special ability, spell or feature explicitly says so. Only one Bonus Action is possible per turn even if several are available. Anything that prevents you from taking actions also prevents a Bonus Action.
Overview.Example: A Rogue attacks with their action and then uses Cunning Action as a Bonus Action to hide.

OffHand.Title: Two-Weapon Attack
OffHand.Subtitle: An extra attack with a weapon that has the Light property.
OffHand.Summary: If you attack with a weapon that has the Light property, you can use your Bonus Action to make one extra attack with a different Light weapon in your other hand. Both weapons must have the Light property. The second attack adds your ability modifier to damage only if that modifier is negative.
OffHand.Example: A Rogue attacks with her Shortsword and uses her Bonus Action for a second attack with her Dagger. The Dagger deals only its weapon die without her Dexterity modifier.
OffHand.Notes: Two-Weapon Fighting depends solely on the Light weapon property and is not tied to a Fighting Style.

Spell.Title: Bonus Action Spell
Spell.Subtitle: Spells whose casting time is a bonus action (e.g. Healing Word).
Spell.Summary: Some spells have a casting time of one Bonus Action and must be cast on your turn. If you cast such a spell, the only spell you may cast as your action in the same turn is a cantrip, not a second leveled spell.
Spell.Example: The Cleric casts Healing Word as a bonus action on the falling Fighter, then in the same turn casts only a cantrip like Sacred Flame, never a second leveled spell.
Spell.Notes: The restriction applies only to leveled spells. Cantrips remain available as your action.

Class.Title: Class Bonus Actions
Class.Subtitle: Class-specific bonus actions — see your class entry.
Class.Summary: Many class features bring their own Bonus Actions. The Rogue has Cunning Action, the Barbarian has Rage, the Monk has its focus features and the Paladin has Divine Smite. Check your class description for the trigger and any usage limit.
Class.Example: A Rogue uses Cunning Action to Disengage as a Bonus Action instead of spending their action on it.

Overview.Title: Reaction
Overview.Subtitle: A once-per-round response to a trigger outside your turn.
Overview.Summary: A Reaction is a special action taken in response to a trigger. You have exactly one Reaction per round, which returns at the start of your next turn. The trigger must be perceivable, and the Reaction resolves immediately after it unless described otherwise.
Overview.Example: A Fighter sees a Goblin shaman casting a spell and uses her reaction for Counterspell — assuming she knows the spell herself.

Subtitle.metric: When a visible enemy leaves your reach, you make one melee attack.
Subtitle.imperial: When a visible enemy leaves your reach, you make one melee attack.

Summary.metric: When a creature you can see leaves your reach using its action, Bonus Action, Reaction or one of its movement modes, you can use your Reaction to make one melee attack with a weapon or an Unarmed Strike against it. The attack occurs right before the creature leaves your reach.
Summary.imperial: When a creature you can see leaves your reach using its action, Bonus Action, Reaction or one of its movement modes, you can use your Reaction to make one melee attack with a weapon or an Unarmed Strike against it. The attack occurs right before the creature leaves your reach.

Example.metric: A Goblin tries to run past the Fighter to reach the Wizard. The Fighter takes her reaction and swings her sword as soon as the Goblin leaves her reach.
Example.imperial: A Goblin tries to run past the Fighter to reach the Wizard. The Fighter takes her reaction and swings her sword as soon as the Goblin leaves her reach.

Notes.metric: The Disengage action prevents opportunity attacks for that turn. A creature you cannot see never triggers an opportunity attack.
Notes.imperial: The Disengage action prevents opportunity attacks for that turn. A creature you cannot see never triggers an opportunity attack.

Ready.Title: Readied Reaction
Ready.Subtitle: A previously readied action triggers now.
Ready.Summary: The Reaction half of the Ready action. When your chosen trigger occurs you spend your Reaction and take the planned action or movement. You may also ignore the trigger. If it does not occur before the start of your next turn, the readying is lost.
Ready.Example: The Archer has readied a draw aimed at the doorframe. As soon as the first Goblin slips through, the reaction triggers — the arrow flies.

Spell.Title: Reaction Spells
Spell.Subtitle: Spells with a casting time of 1 reaction — Shield, Feather Fall, Counterspell.
Spell.Summary: Some spells have a casting time of 1 reaction tied to a specific trigger described in the spell. They consume a slot (cantrips none) and your reaction this round. Remember: only one reaction per round — if you cast Shield as a reaction, you have no reaction left until the start of your next turn.
Spell.Example: The Wizard is hit by an arrow that would just barely beat her AC. She casts Shield as a reaction: +5 AC until the start of her next turn — the arrow misses.

Subtitle.metric: Your speed defines how far you can move in a single turn.
Subtitle.imperial: Your speed defines how far you can move in a single turn.

Summary.metric: On your turn you have movement equal to your Speed, which is 9 metres for most player characters. You may freely interleave movement with your action, Bonus Action and object interactions, and split it into several stretches. Unused movement is lost at the end of your turn.
Summary.imperial: On your turn you have movement equal to your Speed, which is 30 feet for most player characters. You may freely interleave movement with your action, Bonus Action and object interactions, and split it into several stretches. Unused movement is lost at the end of your turn.

Example.metric: A Halfling Rogue with 7.5 m of speed moves 4.5 m forward, attacks a Goblin, then slips 3 m behind a column.
Example.imperial: A Halfling Rogue with 25 ft of speed moves 15 ft forward, attacks a Goblin, then slips 10 ft behind a column.

Subtitle.metric: Each metre of movement there costs one extra metre.
Subtitle.imperial: Each foot of movement there costs one extra foot.

Summary.metric: If a space is Difficult Terrain, every metre of movement in it costs one extra metre. Moving 1.5 metres through Difficult Terrain therefore costs 3 metres of movement. Difficult Terrain is not cumulative: a space either is Difficult Terrain or it is not, and multiple causes do not raise the cost further.
Summary.imperial: If a space is Difficult Terrain, every foot of movement in it costs one extra foot. Moving 5 feet through Difficult Terrain therefore costs 10 feet of movement. Difficult Terrain is not cumulative: a space either is Difficult Terrain or it is not, and multiple causes do not raise the cost further.

Example.metric: A Wizard with 9 metres of Speed crosses a 4.5 metre rubble field. It costs her 9 metres, all of her movement for the turn.
Example.imperial: A Wizard with 30 feet of Speed crosses a 15 foot rubble field. It costs her 30 feet, all of her movement for the turn.

Subtitle.metric: Long Jump: Strength score divided by 3 in metres. High Jump: (3 + Strength modifier) divided by 3.
Subtitle.imperial: Long Jump: Strength score in feet. High Jump: 3 + Strength modifier in feet.

Summary.metric: With a Long Jump you leap horizontally a number of metres equal to your Strength score divided by 3, provided you moved at least 3 metres immediately before. With a High Jump you reach (3 plus your Strength modifier) divided by 3 metres. From a standing start both are halved. Each metre jumped costs a metre of movement. Landing in Difficult Terrain requires a DC 10 Acrobatics check or you gain the Prone condition.
Summary.imperial: With a Long Jump you leap horizontally a number of feet equal to your Strength score, provided you moved at least 10 feet immediately before. With a High Jump you reach 3 plus your Strength modifier in feet. From a standing start both are halved. Each foot jumped costs a foot of movement. Landing in Difficult Terrain requires a DC 10 Acrobatics check or you gain the Prone condition.

Example.metric: A Barbarian with Strength 18 takes a running start and clears 6 metres across a chasm, since 18 divided by 3 is 6.
Example.imperial: A Barbarian with Strength 18 takes a running start and clears 18 feet across a chasm, since the Strength score equals the distance in feet.

Notes.metric: A low obstacle in your path may require a DC 10 Athletics check. During the jump you can reach up half your height above yourself.
Notes.imperial: A low obstacle in your path may require a DC 10 Athletics check. During the jump you can reach up half your height above yourself.

Subtitle.metric: Each metre costs one extra metre unless you have a Climb Speed.
Subtitle.imperial: Each foot costs one extra foot unless you have a Climb Speed.

Summary.metric: While climbing, each metre of movement costs one extra metre, or two extra metres in Difficult Terrain. You ignore this extra cost if you have a Climb Speed and use it. On a slippery surface or one with few handholds the DM may require a DC 15 Athletics check.
Summary.imperial: While climbing, each foot of movement costs one extra foot, or two extra feet in Difficult Terrain. You ignore this extra cost if you have a Climb Speed and use it. On a slippery surface or one with few handholds the DM may require a DC 15 Athletics check.

Example.metric: A Rogue climbs 4.5 metres up a building wall. It costs him 9 metres, his entire Speed for the turn.
Example.imperial: A Rogue climbs 15 feet up a building wall. It costs him 30 feet, his entire Speed for the turn.

Subtitle.metric: Each metre costs one extra metre unless you have a Swim Speed.
Subtitle.imperial: Each foot costs one extra foot unless you have a Swim Speed.

Summary.metric: While swimming, each metre of movement costs one extra metre, or two extra metres in Difficult Terrain. A Swim Speed removes this extra cost. Moving any distance in rough water may require a DC 15 Athletics check.
Summary.imperial: While swimming, each foot of movement costs one extra foot, or two extra feet in Difficult Terrain. A Swim Speed removes this extra cost. Moving any distance in rough water may require a DC 15 Athletics check.

Example.metric: A Wizard swims across a calm river. Covering 4.5 metres costs him 9 metres of movement. In a storm an Athletics check would be added.
Example.imperial: A Wizard swims across a calm river. Covering 15 feet costs him 30 feet of movement. In a storm an Athletics check would be added.

Subtitle.metric: While prone, each metre costs one extra metre.
Subtitle.imperial: While prone, each foot costs one extra foot.

Summary.metric: While crawling, each metre of movement costs one extra metre, or two extra metres in Difficult Terrain. Crawling and standing up are your only movement options while you have the Prone condition.
Summary.imperial: While crawling, each foot of movement costs one extra foot, or two extra feet in Difficult Terrain. Crawling and standing up are your only movement options while you have the Prone condition.

Example.metric: A Cleric lies on the ground and crawls 1.5 metres to the fallen Fighter. That costs 3 metres of her 9 metre Speed.
Example.imperial: A Cleric lies on the ground and crawls 5 feet to the fallen Fighter. That costs 10 feet of her 30 foot Speed.

Subtitle.metric: 1d6 bludgeoning damage per 3 m fallen, capped at 20d6.
Subtitle.imperial: 1d6 bludgeoning damage per 10 ft fallen, capped at 20d6.

Summary.metric: A falling creature takes 1d6 bludgeoning damage at the end of the fall for every 3 metres fallen, up to a maximum of 20d6. On landing it gains the Prone condition unless it avoids all damage from the fall. A creature falling into water or another liquid can use its Reaction to make a DC 15 Athletics or Acrobatics check, halving the damage on a success.
Summary.imperial: A falling creature takes 1d6 bludgeoning damage at the end of the fall for every 10 feet fallen, up to a maximum of 20d6. On landing it gains the Prone condition unless it avoids all damage from the fall. A creature falling into water or another liquid can use its Reaction to make a DC 15 Athletics or Acrobatics check, halving the damage on a success.

Example.metric: A Rogue falls 9 m and takes 3d6 bludgeoning damage — landing prone.
Example.imperial: A Rogue falls 30 ft and takes 3d6 bludgeoning damage — landing prone.

Notes.metric: The Prone condition is avoided only if the fall damage is negated entirely, for example by Feather Fall.
Notes.imperial: The Prone condition is avoided only if the fall damage is negated entirely, for example by Feather Fall.

Subtitle.metric: Standing up costs half your Speed, rounded down.
Subtitle.imperial: Standing up costs half your Speed, rounded down.

Summary.metric: While you have the Prone condition, standing up costs movement equal to half your Speed, rounded down, and ends the condition. If your Speed is 0 you cannot stand up. If your remaining movement is not enough, you must stay prone or crawl.
Summary.imperial: While you have the Prone condition, standing up costs movement equal to half your Speed, rounded down, and ends the condition. If your Speed is 0 you cannot stand up. If your remaining movement is not enough, you must stay prone or crawl.

Example.metric: A Fighter with 9 metres of Speed stands up from prone for 4.5 metres and uses the remaining 4.5 metres to reach the Goblin.
Example.imperial: A Fighter with 30 feet of Speed stands up from prone for 15 feet and uses the remaining 15 feet to reach the Goblin.

Blinded.Title: Blinded
Blinded.Subtitle: You cannot see — attacks against you have advantage, your attacks have disadvantage.
Blinded.Summary: You cannot see and automatically fail any check that requires sight. Attack rolls against you have Advantage, and your own attack rolls have Disadvantage.
Blinded.Example: A Wizard is blinded by a Dust Devil. He misses the Storm Giant twice with Disadvantage while the giant lands its blow with Advantage.
Blinded.Notes: Senses such as Blindsight or Tremorsense can offset the effect where their description says so.

Charmed.Title: Charmed
Charmed.Subtitle: You cannot attack the charmer; they have advantage on social checks against you.
Charmed.Summary: You cannot attack the charmer or target them with damaging abilities or magical effects. The charmer also has Advantage on any check to interact with you socially. Otherwise you remain fully capable.
Charmed.Example: A Dryad casts Charm Person on the Fighter. He cannot attack the Dryad, but her Goblin guards are still fair game.
Charmed.Notes: Charmed does not turn you into a puppet. It only shields the charmer from your attacks and grants them a social edge.

Deafened.Title: Deafened
Deafened.Subtitle: You cannot hear — auditory checks fail automatically.
Deafened.Summary: You cannot hear and automatically fail any check that requires hearing. You can still cast spells with verbal components as long as you can speak.
Deafened.Example: A Bard is deafened by a Thunderclap. He cannot hear the approaching Rogues, losing the edge their loud footsteps would have given him.
Deafened.Notes: Telepathy is unaffected by Deafened, as it bypasses hearing entirely.

Frightened.Title: Frightened
Frightened.Subtitle: You roll with disadvantage while you can see the source, and cannot willingly approach it.
Frightened.Summary: While the source of your fear is in your line of sight you have Disadvantage on ability checks and attack rolls. You also cannot willingly move closer to the source. Breaking line of sight removes the Disadvantage but not the condition.
Frightened.Example: A Dragon uses its Frightful Presence. The Fighter fails the save, backs away and attacks the next round only with Disadvantage.
Frightened.Notes: The penalties depend purely on line of sight. Taking cover removes them without ending the condition.

Grappled.Title: Grappled
Grappled.Subtitle: Speed 0; attacks against targets other than the grappler have Disadvantage.
Grappled.Summary: Your Speed is 0 and cannot be increased. You have Disadvantage on attack rolls against any target other than the grappler. The grappler can drag or carry you when moving, but each foot costs them one extra foot unless you are Tiny or much smaller.
Grappled.Example: A Giant Crab grabs the Fighter with its claw. The Fighter is grappled, cannot move, and can only meaningfully attack the crab itself.
Grappled.Notes: The grapple comes from the Grapple option of the Unarmed Strike. The escape DC is 8 plus the grappler's Strength modifier and Proficiency Bonus.

Incapacitated.Title: Incapacitated
Incapacitated.Subtitle: No actions, no bonus actions, no reactions. You also lose concentration on spells.
Incapacitated.Summary: You cannot take an action, Bonus Action or Reaction. Your Concentration is broken and you cannot speak. If you are Incapacitated when you roll Initiative, you have Disadvantage on the roll.
Incapacitated.Example: A Wizard is caught by Hold Person. He is Paralyzed and therefore Incapacitated, so his Concentration spell Bless ends at once.
Incapacitated.Notes: Incapacitated is a building block inside Paralyzed, Petrified, Stunned and Unconscious.

Invisible.Title: Invisible
Invisible.Subtitle: Others cannot see you; attacks have advantage/disadvantage in your favor.
Invisible.Summary: You are not affected by effects that require a visible target, and neither is the equipment you wear or carry. Attack rolls against you have Disadvantage and your own have Advantage. If a creature can somehow see you, you lose that Advantage against it. Rolling Initiative while Invisible gives you Advantage on the roll.
Invisible.Example: A Monk drinks a potion of invisibility, sneaks up on a cultist, and attacks with advantage — the first strike reveals her position.
Invisible.Notes: The Hide action grants this condition on a successful Stealth check against DC 15.

Paralyzed.Title: Paralyzed
Paralyzed.Subtitle: Incapacitated + immobile. Hits within reach are automatic critical hits.
Paralyzed.Summary: You have the Incapacitated condition, and your Speed is 0 and cannot be increased. Strength and Dexterity saving throws fail automatically. Attack rolls against you have Advantage, and any hit from within 5 feet is automatically a Critical Hit.
Paralyzed.Example: A Deep Wizard is paralyzed by a spell. The enemy Fighter swings in melee — every hit is automatically critical.
Paralyzed.Notes: Because Paralyzed includes Incapacitated, Concentration on ongoing spells also breaks.

Petrified.Title: Petrified
Petrified.Subtitle: Turned to stone. Heavy resistances, but Strength/Dex saves fail automatically.
Petrified.Summary: You and your nonmagical possessions turn into a solid inanimate substance, your weight increases tenfold and you stop aging. You have the Incapacitated condition, your Speed is 0, and Strength and Dexterity saving throws fail automatically. You have Resistance to all damage and Immunity to the Poisoned condition.
Petrified.Example: A Wizard is hit by a Basilisk's gaze, fails the saving throw, and is petrified. Until a healing spell intervenes, he is out of the fight.
Petrified.Notes: Petrification does not end through ordinary healing. It takes magic such as Greater Restoration.

Poisoned.Title: Poisoned
Poisoned.Subtitle: Attack rolls and ability checks have disadvantage.
Poisoned.Summary: You have Disadvantage on attack rolls and ability checks. Saving throws are unaffected. Duration and ending depend on the effect that caused it.
Poisoned.Example: A Rogue is bitten by a spider — she fails the first saving throw and is poisoned for an hour, with disadvantage on every attack.
Poisoned.Notes: Resistance to poison damage does not protect against the Poisoned condition. That requires Immunity to the condition itself.

Subtitle.metric: Only crawling or standing up; melee attacks against you have Advantage.
Subtitle.imperial: Only crawling or standing up; melee attacks against you have Advantage.

Summary.metric: Your only movement options are to crawl or to stand up, which costs half your Speed and ends the condition. You have Disadvantage on attack rolls. An attack roll against you has Advantage if the attacker is within 1.5 metres, otherwise it has Disadvantage.
Summary.imperial: Your only movement options are to crawl or to stand up, which costs half your Speed and ends the condition. You have Disadvantage on attack rolls. An attack roll against you has Advantage if the attacker is within 5 feet, otherwise it has Disadvantage.

Example.metric: A Fighter is shoved to the ground. The Goblins in melee attack with Advantage, while the archer further away attacks with Disadvantage.
Example.imperial: A Fighter is shoved to the ground. The Goblins in melee attack with Advantage, while the archer further away attacks with Disadvantage.

Notes.metric: If your Speed is 0 you cannot stand up. Unconscious and Petrified include the Prone condition.
Notes.imperial: If your Speed is 0 you cannot stand up. Unconscious and Petrified include the Prone condition.

Restrained.Title: Restrained
Restrained.Subtitle: Speed 0; attacks against you have Advantage, Dexterity saves Disadvantage.
Restrained.Summary: Your Speed is 0 and cannot be increased. Attack rolls against you have Advantage and your own have Disadvantage. You also have Disadvantage on Dexterity saving throws.
Restrained.Example: A Rogue is restrained by Entangle. He cannot reach the Goblin archer, rolls his Dexterity saves with Disadvantage and is easy prey in melee.
Restrained.Notes: Restrained hits harder than Grappled: only here do attacks against you have Advantage and your Dexterity saves Disadvantage.

Stunned.Title: Stunned
Stunned.Subtitle: Incapacitated, speed 0, Strength/Dex saves fail automatically.
Stunned.Summary: You have the Incapacitated condition. Strength and Dexterity saving throws fail automatically, and attack rolls against you have Advantage.
Stunned.Example: A Monk stuns a Goblin that fails its save. The Rogue immediately uses the Advantage for a Sneak Attack.
Stunned.Notes: As a consequence of Incapacitated, Concentration on ongoing spells breaks here too.

Subtitle.metric: Incapacitated and Prone; hits from within 1.5 metres are critical.
Subtitle.imperial: Incapacitated and Prone; hits from within 5 feet are critical.

Summary.metric: You have the Incapacitated and Prone conditions and drop whatever you are holding. Your Speed is 0. Strength and Dexterity saving throws fail automatically, attack rolls against you have Advantage, and any hit from within 1.5 metres is a Critical Hit.
Summary.imperial: You have the Incapacitated and Prone conditions and drop whatever you are holding. Your Speed is 0. Strength and Dexterity saving throws fail automatically, attack rolls against you have Advantage, and any hit from within 5 feet is a Critical Hit.

Example.metric: A Fighter drops to 0 hit points and falls unconscious. He drops his sword, lies on the ground and rolls death saving throws.
Example.imperial: A Fighter drops to 0 hit points and falls unconscious. He drops his sword, lies on the ground and rolls death saving throws.

Notes.metric: When the Unconscious condition ends you remain Prone and must stand up normally.
Notes.imperial: When the Unconscious condition ends you remain Prone and must stand up normally.

Exhaustion.Title: Exhaustion
Exhaustion.Intro: Exhaustion is cumulative: each time you gain it your Exhaustion level rises by 1. Each level reduces every D20 Test by 2 and your Speed by {unitStep}. At level 6 you die.
Exhaustion.Notes: Finishing a Long Rest removes 1 Exhaustion level. When your level reaches 0 the condition ends. Magic such as Greater Restoration removes a level instantly.

Calendar.Intro: A year in the Calendar of Harptos has 365 days. It is made up of 12 months of 30 days each (3 tendays). Between certain months sit 5 special holidays that do not count as month days. Every 4 years adds Shieldmeet after Midsummer as a 6th leap-year holiday.

Holiday.MidwinterDesc: Holiday between Hammer and Alturiak — the cold middle of winter.
Holiday.GreengrassDesc: Holiday between Tarsakh and Mirtul — the first day of spring.
Holiday.MidsummerDesc: Holiday between Flamerule and Eleasis — summer solstice.
Holiday.ShieldmeetDesc: Leap-year holiday right after Midsummer, every 4 years — day of great gatherings and oaths.
Holiday.HighharvestDesc: Holiday between Eleint and Marpenoth — harvest festival and end of high summer.
Holiday.MoonfestDesc: Holiday between Uktar and Nightal — day of remembrance for the dead.
